newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. tribunal soldiers on despite Bosnia inertia.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tribunal soldiers on despite Bosnia inertia.

text.p: The U.N. tribunal for former Yugoslavia, fighting growing apathy about crimes committed years ago in the Balkan war, claimed Wednesday's conviction of a Bosnian Serb for persecution of Moslems as an important victory for justice.
Chief prosecutor Louise Arbour said the verdict against Dusan Tadic captured both his legal and his moral culpability.
"You have been witnesses today to justice being done and justice being seen to be done," she told reporters.
Despite Arbour's upbeat tone, the first international war crimes court since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials 50 years ago continues to fight an arduous uphill battle.

Four years after it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, the tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals, including the former Bosnian Serb political and military leaders, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both of whom face genocide charges.
However, the vast majority remain at large and so far only eight have been arrested and sent for trial in The Hague.
Arbour said international support for the tribunal had been disappointing, but that the Tadic verdict might change this.
"The record to date is one of considerable inertia by the international community. I'd like to think that today will be a stepping stone to displacing some of that inertia," she said.
Human Rights Watch said the Tadic verdict should serve as a reminder of the need to bring to justice all of those indicted for the worst crimes in Europe since World War Two.

"Much more needs to be done if the tribunal is to fulfill its promise of justice based on individualised responsibility, as opposed to violent revenge based on the false assumption of collective ethnic guilt," the group said in a statement.
Appalled by the horrors of the Bosnian conflict in the early 1990s, western countries pressed for the tribunal to be set up to try those held responsible for some of the worst excesses.
But since the Dayton peace agreement was signed in 1995, the same countries have refused to risk the lives of their troops in Bosnia by trying to capture the men sought by the tribunal.
Authorities in the former Yugoslavia have also shown little inclination to arrest and extradite indicted war crimes suspects, though Bosnia and Croatia have turned in a handful.
As time passes, the prospect of bringing more of the accused into the tribunal's trial chamber seems increasingly remote.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, visiting the tribunal in March, described the situation as a bizarre waiting game.
"Obviously it is frustrating to sit and wait for indicted criminals to be tried who haven't come. It's like waiting for Godot," he said.

Tribunal president Antonio Cassesse said in March that the lack of political will to arrest suspected war criminals posed a serious threat: "The general picture for the future of the tribunal is not too rosy," he said.
Despite the problems it has faced, academics and diplomats said the Yugoslavia tribunal had been valuable in signalling the world's disapproval of the excesses of the Balkan war.
Its creation had also helped along efforts within the U.N. to set up a permanent international criminal court, they said.
Arbour said she hoped the verdict would encourage the world to take measures to ensure other suspects "more culpable or equally culpable" would eventually be brought to justice.
But Britain, while expressing strong support for the tribunal, placed the onus firmly on the former Yugoslav republics to arrest and deliver suspects to The Hague.
"We continue to press the states in the region to surrender their indictees," a Foreign Office statement released through the British embassy in The Hague said.
